performanceBudget.why: F0 committed absolute millisecond ceilings; F6 has to certify 'no regression beyond the F0 budget' on hosts F0 never ran on. A millisecond is a property of the machine, so the enforced budget here is a RATIO against a reference workload measured in the same process, on the same driver, in the same run. Absolute ceilings survive as a secondary catastrophe check and may never be looser than the F0 file they descend from.

measuredOn.sensitivityNote: Ceilings are 2.0x the worst of the eight calibration runs, so the gate trips somewhere between a 2.0x regression (measured on a bad run) and a 2.8x one (measured on a good run). That is the honest sensitivity: it catches the N+1 query, the lost index, the second sanitisation pass and the synchronous flush, and it does not catch a 20% slowdown. Chasing 20% on a shared runner buys false failures, not information.
measuredOn.provisionalMargin: The 2.0x factor is 1.5x for measurement noise TIMES a deliberate allowance for calibrating on one platform only. The denominator is ten autocommit inserts while the numerators are transactions, so the ratio is sensitive to how expensive a per-statement durability flush is on the host filesystem; Windows pays more for that than ext4, which inflates the denominator here and would make a Windows-tight ceiling flap on a Linux runner. This looseness is recorded rather than hidden: once the harness has run on the CI host, record that observation and tighten the ceilings back toward 1.5x.

methodology.note: observedRatioToReference records the WORST of the calibration runs and every ceiling sits at 2.0x it (see measuredOn.provisionalMargin for why not 1.5x). ceilingMarginRange is the window a ceiling must stay inside relative to its own recorded observation: below 1.2x it flaps on a loaded host and gets disabled within a week, above 3.0x nothing can fail it, which is the same defect as having no threshold. Loosening a ceiling therefore forces re-recording the observation beside it — a visible act in review rather than a one-character edit.

reference.workload: ten single-row INSERTs through the active driver
reference.why: Content operations are driver-bound, so a reference that is itself ten durable writes moves with the host and with the driver. Three candidate denominators were measured side by side in the same six runs — a single INSERT+SELECT round trip, fifty SELECT 1 round trips, and this ten-insert batch — and the batch produced the tightest run-to-run ratios (worst spread 1.24x against 1.35x and 1.33x). It is also large enough (~0.37ms) that timer jitter is not a meaningful share of the denominator, which a 6us SELECT 1 could not claim.
reference.boundsNote: The denominator is load-bearing in both directions. A reference that collapses (writes that stopped being durable) deflates nothing but inflates every ratio into a red run with a confusing message; a reference that inflates deflates every ratio and the gate would pass a real regression. Both bounds are deliberately wide — they exist to catch a change in the driver write path, not to judge the host.

contentRender.note: The rendering operation the F6 plan names had no ceiling anywhere: f0-performance-budgets.json budgets create, update, meta, revision and list, and nothing renders. f0BudgetKey is null because there is no F0 entry to inherit from, not because the ceiling is optional.

httpSteadyState.why: The in-process budget above covers the backend render step. The end-to-end page render is HTTP, so scripts/perf-bench.mjs enforces the same shape there: every target expressed as a ratio to /healthz measured in the same run. /healthz is the right denominator because it is the whole HTTP stack — listener, middleware chain, event loop, JSON encode — doing no application work.

reference.note: Root-level, no database, excluded from the rate limiter.

httpSteadyState.calibration: UNCALIBRATED, and the first attempt to calibrate found two reasons it must stay that way until this budget is redesigned. `npm run perf:bench:enforce` therefore still FAILS with an instruction rather than reporting green on evidence that does not support it — a ratio nobody measured must not pass, and skipping the uncalibrated entries is the failure mode this programme has already had to fix twice. See firstCleanObservation for what was measured, and reference.note for the two defects.

whyNotRecordedAsCalibration: THE DENOMINATOR HAS NO RESOLUTION. /healthz reports p95 = 1ms and autocannon reports latency in whole milliseconds, so every ratio is the target p95 divided by 1 — it EQUALS the absolute p95 and normalises nothing between machines, which is the only reason this budget is expressed as a ratio at all. Quantising a 1ms denominator carries up to a 2x error by itself. The in-process budget above avoided exactly this by choosing a ten-insert batch large enough that timer jitter is not a meaningful share of it (see reference.why); the HTTP reference needs the same treatment.

ONE RUN IS ALL THE RATE LIMITER ALLOWS. methodology.note requires the WORST of several runs. This run was clean (non2xx = 0); three further runs in the same 15-minute window returned ~20000 non-2xx each, and their API rows measured the limiter rather than the route — settings 'improved' from 230ms to 5ms. Calibrating needs runs spaced past the 1000-request window, or the bench exempted from the limiter.
firstCleanObservation.note: Kept because a measurement that exists beats a blank, and because settings at 230ms p95 / 43 req-per-second is worth looking at on its own terms.
